Hi Danielle — thanks again for the call today. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we're all aligned: 

Summary of asks from your side:
- Latency targets: p95 <= 200ms for short prompts, p95 <= 500ms for longer streaming responses
- Throughput/concurrency: normal concurrency ~80-120 rps, spikes up to ~250 rps for 30–60s
- Streaming: ~40% of requests use streaming (token-by-token) and must maintain low tail latency
- Availability: business-critical endpoints should have an SLO-backed SLA

Initial Redwood recommendations (for discussion):
- Warm pool: 4 prewarmed GPU instances for primary endpoint to absorb short spikes; keep 1–2 reserve nodes for burst
- Scale-up: target cold-to-warm add time <= 60s for queued requests; with warm pool hit rate we can keep user-observed scale latency under the p95 target
- Queueing policy: soft-queue with depth 100 requests and FIFO for short sync requests; streaming requests prioritize token flushes
- Fallbacks: auto-fallback to lower-cost quantized model for non-streaming longer-running jobs to preserve SLA during extended load

Attachments: I'm attaching a first-pass SLO matrix (slo_matrix-fastpay.xlsx) that maps endpoints, p50/p95 targets and suggested warm-pool sizes.

Next steps:
1) Can you share a 24–48h traffic sample (spike windows highlighted) — will help us size warm pools more precisely (fastpay_traffic_sample.csv would work).
2) Vivek to do a short tech note on warm-pool costs and scale-up mechanics (we'll loop him in).
3) Schedule a 30-min tech deep-dive next week to agree on the mutual action plan.

If the above looks good I'll lock a tentative Wed or Thu slot.

Thanks —

Hi all — quick technical note while we prepare for the deep-dive. Thanks for the traffic sample, Danielle — that's very useful. A few concrete notes / tradeoffs to consider: 

1) Warm-pool sizing
- Recommendation: start with 4 prewarmed GPUs (same instance type as production) for the primary low-latency endpoint. Based on your burst patterns a 4-node pool gives ~1.5–2x baseline headroom and significantly reduces user-visible p95 during short spikes.
- Cost tradeoff: warm instances incur steady-state hourly costs; we can run a cost simulation vs observed spike frequency to show break-even.

2) Scale-up times & queueing
- Cold scale-up (provision + model load): 45–90s depending on image and model size.
- Warm-pool add (hot instance already provisioned): 10–30s to attach to serving mesh and begin accepting traffic.
- Queue policy: recommend soft queue with max depth 100; beyond that we surface a 429 to keep latency SLOs for in-flight requests. We can tune the depth per endpoint.

3) Streaming behavior
- Streaming requests are latency-sensitive for token flushes. We prioritize streaming sockets across the pool and reserve 20% of concurrency slots for streaming to avoid head-of-line blocking.
- If the pool is saturated we can route new streaming sessions to a smaller, lower-cost streaming-optimized model with identical token-by-token behavior (but lower throughput) as a graceful degradation.

4) Warm-pool warmup strategies
- Keep a small number of warm replicas with loaded KV cache and warmed CUDA kernels to reduce first-token latency.
- For predictable campaign windows we can schedule warm-ups (cron-based) to avoid cold-starts.

5) Next steps for the deep dive
- I'll prepare a short runbook: warm-pool sizing calculation, cost simulation, and a diagram of routing/queueing (attached: autoscale-diagram.png).
- Please confirm a Wed 10:00–10:30 AM PST slot and any specific endpoints you want to test in the runbook.

Cheers,
